89: The function you write does not return the text itself. It returns another function.
A function can be returned like any other value, for example with an arrow function: `() => ...`.
Return an inner function whose body just returns "Hello World". It does not need any parameters.
90: The counter has to remember where it is between calls. Where could that number live so it survives after each call ends?
This is a closure: a variable declared in the outer function stays alive for the inner function that is returned.
Keep `let count = n` in the outer function. The inner function returns the current `count` and then increases it (`count++` does both in the right order).
91: First decide what `expect(val)` hands back: an object, so that you can write `expect(5).toBe(...)`.
The object has two methods. Both can use `val` from the outer function (a closure). Each one either returns `true` or throws.
In `toBe`: `if (val === other) return true;` otherwise `throw new Error(...)` with the exact message from the description. `notToBe` is the mirror image.
92: Three functions need to read and change the same number. Where can they all see it?
Declare `let value = init` inside `createCounter`, then return an object whose methods use and change `value` (closure).
Each method updates `value` (`value++`, `value--`, or `value = init`) and then returns `value`. Watch out: `value++` returns the OLD value, so update first and return after.
93: Build a fresh array and fill it while you walk through the old one. Your own array is the "result".
A plain `for` loop over the indexes works well, because you also need the index to give to `fn`.
Create `result = []`. For each index `i`, call `fn(arr[i], i)` and push what it returns into `result`. Return `result` at the end.
94: Walk through the array and decide, item by item, whether it goes into a new array.
Use a `for` loop and an `if`. You need the index too, because `fn` receives it as the second argument.
Create `result = []`. For each index `i`, if `fn(arr[i], i)` is truthy, push `arr[i]` into `result`. Return `result`.
95: Think of a running total that you update as you go through the array. That is the "accumulator".
Declare `let accumulator = init`, then loop over the array with `for` / `for...of` and update the accumulator each time.
For each item: `accumulator = fn(accumulator, item)`. When the loop ends (or immediately, for an empty array) return `accumulator`.
96: Just like in maths, f(g(h(x))): the LAST function in the list gets the input first.
You return a function that takes `x`. Inside it, pass the value through the list of functions, going from the end of the array to the start.
Set `let value = x`. Loop `i` from `functions.length - 1` down to `0` and do `value = functions[i](value)`. Return `value`. With no functions, the loop does nothing, so you get `x` back.
97: The `...args` in the signature already collects every argument for you.
`...args` is a real array, and arrays know their own size.
98: The wrapper has to remember whether it has already been called.
Use a closure: a variable outside the returned function (like a `called` flag). Use `...args` to pass the arguments through to `fn`.
Return a function `(...args) => {...}`. If the flag is already set, return `undefined`. Otherwise set the flag, then return `fn(...args)`.
99: Inside a method, `this` is the array you called it on. Use `this` the way you would use a normal array variable.
Use a normal `function () {}` (not an arrow function), because arrow functions do not have their own `this`. The last index is `this.length - 1`.
First check whether `this.length` is 0 and return -1 if so. Otherwise return the element at index `this.length - 1`.
100: A Promise is the right tool for "do something later": it resolves when you tell it to.
`new Promise((resolve) => ...)` gives you a `resolve` function. `setTimeout` can call it after a delay.
